subject: Computer Networking
title: Cloud Computing Takes Over
description: A fast breakdown of Cloud Computing Takes Over for builders.

hook.text: In 2006, Amazon launched AWS. Rent a server by the hour instead of buying one. Computing became a utility.

buildup.text: Cloud providers built massive data centers connected by private fiber networks spanning continents.

discovery.text: Startups no longer needed server rooms. They could launch globally on day one with a credit card.

twist.text: The cloud created new networking challenges: latency between regions, data sovereignty, and massive east-west traffic.

climax.text: Today, most internet services run in the cloud. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud carry a huge share of global traffic.

punchline.text: Cloud computing moved servers off-site but kept the world connected.

quiz.question: What did Amazon launch in 2006 that transformed computing?

details.summary: Cloud computing, pioneered by Amazon Web Services in 2006, shifted infrastructure from owned hardware to rented computing resources accessed over the internet. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud now host a massive share of internet services, fundamentally changing how software is built and deployed.
details.whyItMatters: Cloud computing eliminated the need to own hardware, democratizing access to computing resources. Startups can now launch with the same infrastructure capabilities as large enterprises.
takeaways: AWS launched in 2006 and pioneered cloud infrastructure
Cloud eliminated the need to purchase and manage servers
Three providers now host a huge share of the internet

faq.question: How did cloud computing change the technology industry?
faq.answer: It eliminated the capital expense of buying servers and the operational burden of managing data centers. Startups could launch with a credit card instead of a server room. Companies could scale resources up and down based on demand rather than purchasing for peak capacity.

faq.question: What risks come with cloud concentration?
faq.answer: When a few cloud providers host most of the internet, their outages affect everyone. AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud outages take down thousands of seemingly independent services. This concentration creates systemic risk that the internet's original design was meant to avoid.
